issues: The 'originator' field states an authorship claim as fact: 'Hippocratic school of Kos'. Modern scholars do not attribute the Oath to Hippocrates. Proposed dates range from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE, and one line of argument (Edelstein) gives it a Pythagorean origin. The NLM page only says the Oath 'may have marked' a move to train people outside 'the Asclepiads of Kos'. The locationNote already hedges ('authorship and exact date are unknown'), so the originator should hedge too.

The note on source[0] gives the date as 'late 5th or 4th century BCE'. That range is too narrow: estimates run from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE, including a Hellenistic dating. 'c. 400 BCE' is still an acceptable conventional displayDate.

This 'control' view runs through later 'notice and choice' rules; Westin himself advised on the US Privacy Act of 1974, and his 1972 Databanks study anticipated the Fair Information Practice Principles.

issues: The originator field credits the concept wholly to the Bundesverfassungsgericht. The court made informational self-determination a constitutional right in 1983, but it did not coin the idea or the term. The 'informationelle Selbstbestimmungsrecht' appears in the July 1971 expert report 'Grundfragen des Datenschutzes' by Wilhelm Steinmüller, Bernd Lutterbeck, Christoph Mallmann and others for the Federal Interior Ministry. That report was printed as Anlage 1 to Bundestag Drucksache VI/3826 (7 September 1972). German Wikipedia ('Informationelle Selbstbestimmung') also says the term goes back to this 1971 report. A primary source is added.

issues: The plainSummary misstates what the law covered. It says the Court struck down 'Connecticut's ban on contraceptive use by married couples', but the statute was not limited to married couples: 'A Connecticut statute makes it a crime for any person to use any drug or article to prevent conception' (syllabus). The Court held it unconstitutional as applied to married couples, grounding the holding in 'the right of marital privacy'. The appellants were convicted as accessories for advising married persons.

fieldFixes.plainSummary: Privacy as freedom to make intimate decisions without the state: the Court strikes down Connecticut's ban on the use of contraceptives as applied to married couples, finding a 'zone of privacy' created by several guarantees in the Bill of Rights.
